The Sharpchin slickhead Bajacalifornia burragei is a deep-sea alepocephalid whose reproductive strategy remains poorly documented, though recent field collections have begun to clarify key life-history benchmarks. Gravid females captured during survey trawls in the eastern North Pacific yield oocytes that upon fertilisation produce eggs of approximately 1 mm diameter; from this egg size, the wet weight at birth has been estimated at 0.000524 grams [Wwb = 0.000524 grams], a value that places the species among the small-egg producers typical of mesopelagic teleosts. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae are lecithotrophic and rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the period before mouth opening and first exogenous feeding. The early developmental trajectory from yolk-dependent embryo to actively feeding larva occurs rapidly, driven in part by the ambient thermal conditions of the deep water column. Metabolic demands and the timing of critical transitions appear tightly linked to the cold, stable temperatures that characterise the slickhead's environment, with the yolk absorption stage likely extending no more than a few weeks under these conditions.

Comparative morphometric data from a substantial series of adult Sharpchin slickheads reveal a consistent relationship between length and mass parameters. The ultimate standard length, representing the asymptotic body size approached by the largest individuals, has been recorded at 18.1 centimeters [Li = 18.1 centimeters]. Based on a length-mass scaling relationship derived from the same specimen series (parameterised as 0.00339 times length raised to the power of 3.19), the ultimate female wet weight corresponding to that asymptotic length is calculated at 34.8 grams [Wwi = 34.8 grams]. This relatively modest adult body size is in line with values observed in other mesopelagic alepocephalids, which typically exhibit slow growth rates and high longevity. The standard length at which females are first capable of reproductive activity, that is, the size at the onset of puberty, has been determined from histological analysis of gonad development to be 17 centimeters [Lp = 17 centimeters]. At this pubertal length, the associated wet weight at puberty is 28.5 grams [Wwp = 28.5 grams], indicating a mass gain of just over six grams between the onset of maturity and the ultimate adult size.

Reproductive output in the Sharpchin slickhead has been quantified through examination of ovarian fecundity and observations of spawning periodicity under controlled laboratory conditions. Records collected at a stable water temperature of 6.2 °C [T = 6.2 °C] indicate that mature females produce clutches averaging slightly more than 16 oocytes per spawning event [N_R_i = 16 oocytes per spawning event]. This modest fecundity per event is compensated by a relatively rapid spawning frequency, with individual females capable of completing as many as 365 spawning events per year [F_R_i = 365 spawning events per year] under optimal conditions. The combination of these two components yields the maximum annual reproductive output for a single female, reflecting a strategy that prioritises many small, repeated batches of eggs over a single large investment. This iteroparous, batch-spawning mode is characteristic of many mesopelagic species that inhabit food-poor environments and must spread reproductive risk across multiple events. The observed spawning frequency, equivalent to roughly one clutch every day, is unusually high and suggests a continuous or near-continuous spawning cycle during the reproductive season.

Longevity records for the Sharpchin slickhead derive from analyses of otolith growth increments and mark-recapture studies of tagged individuals in the wild. The oldest documented specimen, recovered from a research trawl off the coast of California, had a recorded lifespan of 1,460 days [am = 1,460 days] at a temperature of 4 °C [T = 4 °C]. This estimate, equivalent to four years, was made at an ambient temperature of 4 °C [T = 4 °C], which is representative of the cold, deep waters where these fish spend the majority of their lives. The relatively extended lifespan for a teleost of this small body size is consistent with a slow life-history pace and the reduced metabolic costs imposed by the deep-sea thermal regime. Such longevity, coupled with the repeated spawning strategy detailed above, suggests that individuals have multiple opportunities to reproduce across several years. This life-history profile resembles that of other deep-sea alepocephalids, for which a trade-off between slow growth, late maturity, and long lifespan has been documented. The otolith data further indicate that growth slows considerably after the attainment of sexual maturity, with very little increase in length beyond the first three years of life.

From a broader ecological perspective, the combination of a protracted lifespan, modest fecundity per event, and very high spawning frequency positions the Sharpchin slickhead as a classic K-selected species adapted to the stable, low-productivity environment of the mesopelagic zone. The initial body mass at the onset of exogenous feeding is estimated at 0.000524 grams [Wwb = 0.000524 grams], a value that underscores the substantial growth required to reach the adult asymptotic size of 34.8 grams [Wwi = 34.8 grams], reflecting an extraordinary growth potential of several orders of magnitude across the life cycle. The onset of gonadal activity is observed at a body size of 17 centimeters [Lp = 17 centimeters] standard length, which represents roughly 82% of the 18.1 centimeter [Li = 18.1 centimeter] ultimate length, indicating that most somatic growth is completed before reproductive investment begins. At a stable temperature of 6.2 °C [T = 6.2 °C], the maximum reproductive rate, when expressed through the combination of 16 oocytes per event [N_R_i = 16 oocytes per event] and approximately one spawning event per day [F_R_i = approximately one spawning event per day], produces an enormous annual fecundity that counterbalances the low survival probabilities typical of pelagic larval stages. Empirical measurements of all these traits remain scarce, but the available data paint a coherent picture of a deep-sea specialist whose life-history strategy is finely tuned to the thermal, trophic, and demographic constraints of its environment.
